title: Move aside, said Shankara
hookLine: in Kashi, Shankara tells a man with four dogs to get out of his way. the man asks: move what?
carry: one self, mistaken for many, like rope for snake
last: OM: THREE SOUNDS AND A SILENCE.

cards: A story told about Shankara. The young teacher has bathed in the Ganges at Kashi and is walking to the temple with his students.
Down the narrow lane comes a man the society of the day treated as an outcaste, with four dogs. Move aside, Shankara says. Get out of the way.
The man doesn't move. Instead he asks: move what, sir? This body, made of food, away from that body, also made of food?
Or the awareness in me away from the awareness in you? Is the sun reflected in the Ganges different from the sun reflected in a puddle in my lane? Shankara stops.

teach.h: THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.
teach.b: The man's question echoes a teacher before Shankara. Tradition places Gaudapada, author of the Mandukya Karika, as the teacher of Shankara's teacher, and Gaudapada gave Advaita one of its best-known pictures.
A rope, not seen clearly in the dark, is imagined as a snake, or a line of water, or other things. When the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining stops.
In the same way, he says, the one self is imagined as all kinds of things; when the self is known, the imagining ends. Notice what he doesn't say.

teach.h: THE SNAKE WAS NEVER APART FROM IT.
teach.b: The snake didn't turn into the rope or crawl away; it was never anything apart from the rope. That's this week in one picture: Shankara's jnana, the knowing that undoes a mix-up, and Gaudapada's rope.
Advaita doesn't say the world is nothing.
It says the world is the one reality, seen wrongly; teachers call this maya. That's why the man in the lane could stop Shankara cold: the line between them was the snake.
Other schools of Vedanta hold the world real, the Lord's own work. Today we sort people into us and them in a heartbeat.
This teaching asks: which of us, exactly, should move?

how: Advaita Vedanta teachers use the rope and the snake to explain how the one reality can be taken for something it isn't, and students of Advaita still study the Manisha Panchakam, traditionally credited to Shankara.

o: a frog-shaped posture held during meditation
a hymn sung to wake the gods at dawn
verses on Om, the three states and the fourth

games.q: the lane and the rope — tap the pairs.
p: what the self is imagined as

s: Gaudapada says the snake turned into the rope
it was never anything apart from the rope. seeing clearly ends the imagining.
in the story, Shankara stopped and bowed to the man
the verses said to come from it call whoever sees the one self in all 'my teacher'.
every school of Vedanta agrees the world is like the snake
other schools hold the world to be real, the work of the Lord.

games.q: the light shows a rope where you saw a snake. Gaudapada asks: where did the snake go? what's his answer?
o: it slithered off before the light came on.
it was never anything apart from the rope.
games.why: when the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining simply stops. nothing went anywhere.

practice: Picture three people you'll see today: someone you love, someone you hardly notice, and someone who irritates you. One at a time, hold each in mind and say silently: the same self.
If you like, let your palms meet for each, the way many Hindus greet one another. If you pray, look for the one you pray to in each face; if you don't, simply notice what shifts.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where a rope seen in the dark as a snake stands for the self taken for all kinds of things.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a rope; in Gaudapada's image, the rope seen in the dark as a snake.

carryVoice: Your line: one self, mistaken for many, like rope for snake. Shankara bowed in the lane. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.17–2.18 (a rope not clearly seen is imagined as a snake, a line of water and so on; when the rope is ascertained the imagining ceases; so with the self)

Manisha Panchakam (traditionally ascribed to Shankara; the meeting with the outcaste and his dogs at Kashi; body from body or awareness from awareness; the sun reflected in the Ganges and in a puddle; refrain: whoever sees the one self in all is my guru)
sources.work: Manisha Panchakam and the hagiographical tradition (paraphrased)
